zh.q: 同一个直流电源，为什么电解氯化铜溶液得到铜和氯气，电解饱和食盐水却得到氢气、氯气和氢氧化钠？
zh.concl: 电解池是把电能直接转化为化学能的装置：使电流通过电解质溶液，在阳极、阴极引起氧化还原反应（教材原话）。
points: 两个实验回答的是同一个问题：通同样的电，不同的溶液里谁先放电。
两台池子的对照就摆在同一屏上，一眼能比。
界面上的电流、时间、产物量都是课件设定（示意读数），教材只说「25% 溶液」「覆盖一层红色的铜」「试纸变蓝」。

zh.q: 接通电源以后，CuCl₂ 溶液的两根石墨棒上各出现了什么？
zh.concl: 通电后 CuCl₂ 溶液在阳极、阴极分别发生氧化、还原反应，生成了 Cu 和 Cl₂：阳极 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ = Cl₂↑（氧化），阴极 Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ = Cu（还原），总反应 Cu²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ =电解= Cu + Cl₂↑（教材原话）。
points: 红色的是铜，从溶液里的 Cu²⁺ 变来，不是石墨棒变了颜色。
气泡是氯气：有刺激性气味，能把碘化钾氧化出碘，淀粉遇碘变蓝——试纸变蓝就是氯气的证据。
「阳极 / 阴极」说的是氧化 / 还原，跟「正极 / 负极」是两套名字（练习 4 的错误项就栽在这里）。

zh.q: 通得更久、或者把电流调大，为什么产物就更多？多了多少？
zh.concl: 通过的电荷量 Q = I·t 决定产物量：每 2 mol 电子在阴极析出 1 mol Cu、在阳极放出 1 mol Cl₂（教材的两个电极反应各是 2e⁻ 一个粒子）。
points: 产物不是「通得越久越深」那种模糊趋势，而是一条直线：时间加倍、产物加倍。
电流加倍、同样的 600 s，产物也加倍——电量才是那个「账」。
25% CuCl₂ 溶液很浓，600 s 只让 c(Cu²⁺) 降 1.7 %，颜色几乎看不出变浅——这就是教材只让你看红铜和试纸的原因。

zh.q: 「通电时离子改作定向运动」——到底谁往哪边走？电子又走哪儿？
zh.concl: 通电时自由运动的离子改作定向运动：阴离子向阳极迁移、阳离子向阴极迁移；电子在外电路从电源负极走向阴极，不进入溶液（教材原话）。
points: 溶液里的导电靠离子搬家，不是电子在溶液里跑。
阳离子朝阴极、阴离子朝阳极——两根箭头一定反向，画成同向就错了。
电子只在导线里走，从电源负极进阴极；进到阴极以后，这条「接力棒」交给 Cu²⁺ 拿到。

zh.q: 同样是石墨电极、同样的电流，换成饱和食盐水，阴极跑出来的为什么不是钠？
zh.concl: 阳极 Cl⁻ 比 OH⁻ 容易失电子、阴极 H⁺ 比 Na⁺ 容易得电子，所以产物是 Cl₂、H₂ 和 NaOH：2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ = Cl₂↑，2H₂O + 2e⁻ = H₂↑ + 2OH⁻，总反应 2Cl⁻ + 2H₂O =电解= Cl₂↑ + H₂↑ + 2OH⁻（教材原话）。
points: 放电顺序：阳极 Cl⁻ 比 OH⁻ 易失电子 → 出 Cl₂（不是 O₂）；阴极 H⁺ 比 Na⁺ 易得电子 → 出 H₂（不是 Na）。
Na⁺ 留在溶液里，和阴极留下的 OH⁻ 组成 NaOH——氯碱工业要的烧碱（工业上在离子交换膜电解槽里做）。
两极各是 2 个电子一个粒子，所以体积比恒为 1 : 1（体积按 25 ℃、Vm = 24.5 L/mol 算；教材标准状况用 22.4 L/mol，验算会小 8.6 %）。

zh.q: 阴极那根棒周围，为什么滴一滴酚酞就红了？
zh.concl: 阴极上是 H⁺ 得电子：2H₂O + 2e⁻ = H₂↑ + 2OH⁻，OH⁻ 留在阴极区，所以显碱性、酚酞变红。CuCl₂ 体系里 Cu²⁺ 先得电子，教材注明「水电离出的少量 H⁺ 和 OH⁻ 并没有参与电极反应」，所以不产生 OH⁻、酚酞不红。
points: 变红不是「酚酞和盐反应」，是阴极反应把 OH⁻ 攒下来了。
红只在阴极附近慢慢扩散，不是整管一起红。
同一个酚酞，滴在 CuCl₂ 体系里不红（Cu²⁺ 先放电，不产生 OH⁻），这一对比正说明「谁先放电决定出什么产物」。

zh.q: 食盐水里有 4 种离子，凭什么偏偏是 Cl⁻ 和 H⁺ 放电？
zh.concl: 放电顺序由「谁容易失 / 得电子」定：阳极 Cl⁻ 比 OH⁻ 容易失去电子，阴极 H⁺ 比 Na⁺ 容易得到电子（教材原话）；Na⁺ 与 OH⁻ 不放电，留在溶液里。
points: 「4 种离子」不是都能放电，先看氧化性 / 还原性的强弱。
阴极表面是 H⁺ 抢到电子，不是 Na⁺——所以出氢气不出钠。
没放电的 Na⁺ 和 OH⁻ 就是产品 NaOH；工业上要靠离子交换膜把 Cl₂ 和 NaOH 隔开。

zh.q: 把阳极的石墨棒换成一块铜片，为什么阳极就没有气泡、试纸也不变蓝了？
zh.concl: 阳极是活性金属时，阳极材料本身比 Cl⁻ 更容易失去电子：Cu − 2e⁻ = Cu²⁺（阳极溶解），阴极仍是 Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ = Cu，总效果是铜从阳极「搬」到阴极——这正是电镀与电解精炼的原理，电镀液浓度不变。
points: 错误操作链：随便换阳极材料 → 阳极自己溶解 → 得不到氯气 → 还以为「电解失效了」。
错在「阳极材料不参与反应」这个默认：石墨是惰性电极，铜是活性电极。
教材是在 CuSO₄ 体系（电镀 / 精炼铜）里讲活性阳极的；这里借来说明：阳极若是活性金属，先溶解的是阳极自己、不再放 Cl₂（不写成教材原话）。

zh.tag: 考核 · 出 29.6 mg 铜
zh.q: 考核：让 ① 池阴极正好析出 29.6 mg 铜，并保持 15 秒
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：产物量只由电量定——m(Cu) = Q·M/(2F)，所以 (0.20 A, 450 s)、(0.50 A, 180 s)、(0.10 A, 900 s)、(0.30 A, 300 s) 都行，只要电量落在 89.6–92.6 C（刻度上就是 Q = 90 C）：电流大、时间短与电流小、时间长，得到的产物一样多。
points: 先把目标电量算出来（约 91.1 C，刻度上就是 Q = 90 C），再挑一组 (I, t)：**电流大、时间短与电流小、时间长都能达标**（0.20 A × 450 s、0.50 A × 180 s、0.10 A × 900 s 都对）。
电流被推大以后产物会超标，要调回去而不是断电重来。
电源被拔掉时产物归零（本课按「断电 = 未通电」处理），要重新接通。

en.q: With the same DC supply, why does electrolyzing CuCl₂ solution give copper and chlorine, while saturated brine gives hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide?
en.concl: An electrolytic cell converts electrical energy directly into chemical energy: passing current through an electrolyte solution causes redox reactions at the anode and cathode (textbook wording).
points: Both experiments answer the same question: with the same current, which species discharges first in different solutions.
The two cells are side by side on one screen so you can compare at a glance.
Current, time and product amounts on screen are lesson settings (illustrative readings); the textbook only says "25% solution", "covered with a layer of red copper" and "the paper turns blue".

en.q: Once the power is on, what appears on each graphite rod in the CuCl₂ solution?
en.concl: With current on, oxidation and reduction occur at the anode and cathode of the CuCl₂ solution, producing Cu and Cl₂: anode 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ = Cl₂↑ (oxidation), cathode Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ = Cu (reduction), overall Cu²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ =electrolysis= Cu + Cl₂↑ (textbook wording).
points: The red is copper, formed from Cu²⁺ in the solution; the graphite rod didn't change color.
The bubbles are chlorine: it has a pungent smell and oxidizes iodide to iodine, which turns starch blue. The blue paper is the evidence for chlorine.
"Anode / cathode" refer to oxidation / reduction, a different pair of names from "positive / negative" (the wrong option in exercise 4 trips on this).

en.q: Why do you get more product if you run longer or raise the current? How much more?
en.concl: The charge passed, Q = I·t, determines the yield: every 2 mol of electrons deposits 1 mol Cu at the cathode and releases 1 mol Cl₂ at the anode (each of the textbook's two electrode reactions is 2e⁻ per particle).
points: The yield isn't a vague "the longer, the more" trend but a straight line: double the time, double the product.
Double the current for the same 600 s and the product also doubles: charge is what keeps the books.
25% CuCl₂ solution is very concentrated, so 600 s only lowers c(Cu²⁺) by 1.7 % and the color barely lightens. That's why the textbook only has you look at the red copper and the test paper.

en.q: "With current on, the ions move in a definite direction." So who goes where, and where do the electrons go?
en.concl: With current on, freely moving ions move in a definite direction: anions migrate to the anode and cations to the cathode; electrons travel in the external circuit from the supply's negative terminal to the cathode and don't enter the solution (textbook wording).
points: Conduction in the solution is ions moving, not electrons running through the solution.
Cations go to the cathode and anions to the anode, so the two arrows must point opposite ways; drawing them the same way is wrong.
Electrons travel only in the wire, from the negative terminal into the cathode; once there, the "baton" is handed to Cu²⁺.

en.q: Same graphite electrodes, same current. Switch to saturated brine, and why isn't it sodium that comes out at the cathode?
en.concl: At the anode Cl⁻ loses electrons more easily than OH⁻, and at the cathode H⁺ gains electrons more easily than Na⁺, so the products are Cl₂, H₂ and NaOH: 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ = Cl₂↑, 2H₂O + 2e⁻ = H₂↑ + 2OH⁻, overall 2Cl⁻ + 2H₂O =electrolysis= Cl₂↑ + H₂↑ + 2OH⁻ (textbook wording).
points: Discharge order: at the anode Cl⁻ loses electrons more easily than OH⁻ → Cl₂ (not O₂); at the cathode H⁺ gains electrons more easily than Na⁺ → H₂ (not Na).
Na⁺ stays in solution and pairs with the OH⁻ left at the cathode to form NaOH, the caustic soda the chlor-alkali industry wants (made industrially in ion-exchange membrane cells).
Each electrode takes 2 electrons per particle, so the volume ratio is always 1 : 1 (volumes at 25 °C, Vm = 24.5 L/mol; the textbook's STP value 22.4 L/mol gives 8.6 % less).

en.q: Why does the solution around the cathode rod turn red with a drop of phenolphthalein?
en.concl: At the cathode H⁺ gains electrons: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ = H₂↑ + 2OH⁻, and OH⁻ is left in the cathode region, so it turns alkaline and phenolphthalein goes red. In the CuCl₂ system Cu²⁺ gains electrons first, and the textbook notes "the small amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻ from water's ionization do not take part in the electrode reactions", so no OH⁻ forms and phenolphthalein stays colorless.
points: The red isn't "phenolphthalein reacting with salt"; the cathode reaction is building up OH⁻.
The red spreads slowly only near the cathode; the whole tube doesn't turn red at once.
The same phenolphthalein stays colorless in the CuCl₂ system (Cu²⁺ discharges first, so no OH⁻ forms). This contrast shows that "who discharges first decides the product".

en.q: Brine has 4 kinds of ions. Why is it Cl⁻ and H⁺ that discharge?
en.concl: The discharge order is set by "who loses / gains electrons more easily": at the anode Cl⁻ loses electrons more easily than OH⁻, and at the cathode H⁺ gains electrons more easily than Na⁺ (textbook wording); Na⁺ and OH⁻ don't discharge and stay in solution.
points: Not all "4 kinds of ions" can discharge; first compare their oxidizing / reducing strength.
At the cathode surface it's H⁺ that grabs the electrons, not Na⁺, so you get hydrogen, not sodium.
The undischarged Na⁺ and OH⁻ are the product NaOH; industry needs an ion-exchange membrane to keep Cl₂ and NaOH apart.

en.q: Replace the graphite anode with a copper strip. Why are there no more bubbles at the anode, and why doesn't the paper turn blue?
en.concl: When the anode is an active metal, the anode material loses electrons more easily than Cl⁻: Cu − 2e⁻ = Cu²⁺ (anode dissolves), while the cathode is still Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ = Cu. The net effect is copper "moving" from anode to cathode, which is exactly how electroplating and electrolytic refining work, and the plating solution's concentration stays constant.
points: Wrong chain of steps: swap the anode material carelessly → the anode dissolves → no chlorine → thinking "electrolysis stopped working".
It fails on the assumption "the anode material doesn't react": graphite is an inert electrode, copper is an active one.

The textbook covers active anodes in the CuSO₄ system (electroplating / refining copper); here we borrow it to show that if the anode is an active metal, the anode itself dissolves first and no Cl₂ is released (not the textbook's wording).

en.q: Assessment: make cell ①'s cathode deposit exactly 29.6 mg of copper and hold for 15 seconds
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: the yield depends only on charge, m(Cu) = Q·M/(2F), so (0.20 A, 450 s), (0.50 A, 180 s), (0.10 A, 900 s) and (0.30 A, 300 s) all work as long as the charge falls in 89.6–92.6 C (Q = 90 C on the scale): high current for a short time and low current for a long time give the same amount of product.
points: First calculate the target charge (about 91.1 C, which is Q = 90 C on the scale), then pick an (I, t) pair: **high current with short time and low current with long time both pass** (0.20 A × 450 s, 0.50 A × 180 s and 0.10 A × 900 s are all correct).
Once the current is pushed up the product overshoots; turn it back rather than cutting the power and starting over.
When the power is unplugged the product resets to zero (this lesson treats "power off = not electrolyzed"), so reconnect it.
